newsitem.title: UK: UK utilities brace for Labour windfall tax.
newsitem.headline: UK utilities brace for Labour windfall tax.

text.p: Britain's utilities already know that if the opposition Labour party wins power at a general election they will face a one-off "windfall" tax, but shares are still likely have a knee-jerk fall short term, analysts said.
Labour's plans to tax what it calls "the excess profits of privatised utilities" have been known for over three years but what remains unclear is the size and scope of such a levy.

Figures as high as 10 billion pounds ($16 billion) have been rumoured with a spread of affected firms stretching from water and electricity firms through gas supplier Centrica Plc, spun off from British Gas this year, to BT and even former airports authority BAA.

Labour officials have refused to be drawn on details of the tax, while its policy document "Vision for Growth" outlines plans for the tax in a section focusing on gas, electricity and water companies.
The party maintains that it is "100 percent convinced there will be no legal, financial or technical obstacles" to its planned levy despite industry lobbying to the contrary.
It has argued that Britain's utilities were sold off too cheaply and have benefited from relatively benign regulation allowing them to stack up heavy profits.
Electricity and water companies, generally seen as core targets of a windfall tax, have underperformed the market for some time and shares are showing around a 20 percent discount, analysts said.

Nigel Hawkins, analyst at Yamaichi, speculates that on a rough calculation based on market value, the 15 electricity groups might be hit by a two billion pound bill, the 10 big water companies with one billion pounds, BT with 1.5 billion pounds and British Gas with 500 million.

"Fear of such a tax is fairly heavily discounted in the share prices," said Gordon Culfeather of Greig Middleton, adding that most water and electricity firms had strong enough balance sheets to cover a levy over their sectors of 3-5 billion pounds.
But that is unlikely to stop shares stumbling in a knee-jerk reaction to a possible Labour victory, analysts said.
"The market will automatically shed value on a Labour win," Culfeather said.
"Without a doubt, the major impact is going to be the windfall tax. A cautious investor would want little exposure until that unknown has gone," he added.

Labour's other plans for utilities, outlined in the September 1996 document Vison for Growth, are largely already in operation on a voluntary basis, analysts said, and are unlikely to have a major impact on the value of the companies.
Labour suggests possible modifications to the regulatory set-up to increase transparency and accountability, including perhaps a board of non-executive directors to aid the regulator.
The party will also consider the merits and downsides of separate stock market listings for utilities which have been taken over or merged, Vision for Growth says.
Labour appears ready to accept the principle of current inflation-related pricing formulae, or RPI-X, but could look at the cost of capital element in the X factor, officials said.

It also wants gas and electricity firms to provide a range of energy efficiency services and plans regulatory guidelines on quality and continuity of supply, which might include targets for cutting leakage and a sliding scale of compensations.

It will also consider requiring utilities to take out insurance against the possibility of paying such compensation, aiming for premiums to provide incentives to companies to avoid breaching supply guidelines.
Analysts said the party, which has only recently modified its traditional pro-nationalisation stance, is likely to view takeovers with greater reluctance than the Conservatives.

It could also be inclined to extend operation of the "golden" special shares in generators National Power and PowerGen, which effectively block their takeovers, beyond liberalisation of the market in 1998.
However, analysts added that a Conservative victory might not bring unbridled joy to utilities.
"They have been in the private sector long enough to be seen as a legitimate target, the government has already closed some of their tax loopholes," said one analyst.
In the last budget, the government brought taxes on long and short-term assets into line, a move which impacted utilities which have large amounts of long-term investment.
"Neither party looks particularly rosy for the utilities," the analyst said. ($ = 0.624 British Pounds)
